section_summary: This section documents natural disasters affecting Japan from 1930 through 1938, beginning with the Izu earthquake and including later earthquakes, typhoons, the Hakodate fire, and catastrophic flooding in Tokyo and Kobe. It records casualties, damage, the safety of American residents, diplomatic condolences, relief contributions, and official concern about disease, reconstruction, military assistance, censorship, and understated casualty figures. The section also contains several cross-referenced or misfiled records concerning Japanese residents in Manchuria, Ethiopian relief, and emigration from disaster-stricken Japanese regions.

subfiles.title: Telegram on the November 1930 Izu earthquake
subfiles.from: William Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the severity and human consequences of the recent earthquake and the delivery of American condolences.
subfiles.summary: Forbes reports approximately 250 deaths but no American casualties. Because the devastated region contained no large cities, he expected material losses to be limited and had sent condolences to the Japanese Foreign Minister.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference and report on the earthquake near Mishima
subfiles.from: William Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Mishima-area earthquake, its damage, alleged prediction, and possible effect on the Tanna Tunnel.
subfiles.summary: The report places the earthquake's center near Mishima on the Izu Peninsula and estimates about 250 deaths, many homeless people, severe cold, and continuing aftershocks. It notes limited damage to foreign-style hotels, recounts a farmer's purportedly precise prediction, and raises the possibility that the costly Tanna Tunnel project might be abandoned.

subfiles.title: Despatch forwarding correspondence on the Izu earthquake
subfiles.from: William Cameron Forbes, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards the American note of sympathy and the Japanese Foreign Office's reply concerning the Izu earthquake.
subfiles.summary: Forbes transmits copies of his November 29 note and the Foreign Office's December reply. He also records his personal donation to the Japanese Red Cross for relief of earthquake sufferers.

subfiles.title: American Embassy note of sympathy for the Izu disaster
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Kijūrō Shidehara, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Conveys the sympathy of the United States government and people following the Izu earthquake and fire.
subfiles.summary: The note expresses profound sympathy for those affected by earthquake and fire on the Izu Peninsula. It praises the courage of the local population and hopes American sympathy will help assuage its grief.

subfiles.title: Japanese Foreign Office reply thanking the United States
subfiles.from: Kijūrō Shidehara, Minister for Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Thanks the United States for its sympathy and Forbes for his contribution to earthquake relief.
subfiles.summary: Shidehara expresses the gratitude of the Japanese government and people for American sympathy concerning the Izu earthquake and fire. He specifically acknowledges Forbes's monetary donation through Kishi and asks that Japan's thanks be conveyed to the American government and people.

subfiles.title: Earthquake in the Yokohama consular district on November 26, 1930
subfiles.from: Charles W. De Vault, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Provides a detailed official account of the November 26 earthquake in Kanagawa and Shizuoka prefectures.
subfiles.summary: De Vault reports 281 deaths, 218 injuries, 781 destroyed houses, and 4,442 partially destroyed houses, with no foreign fatalities. Nirayama suffered the heaviest damage, while well-built structures, foreign hotels, and railways largely survived; the Tanna Tunnel was faulted but reportedly would not be abandoned.

subfiles.title: Japan Times photographs of the Izu earthquake
subfiles.from: The Japan Times
subfiles.about: Presents early newspaper photographs from the earthquake-stricken Izu Peninsula.
subfiles.summary: The clipping is a morning extra and photographic spread showing the affected area shortly after the earthquake. Its surviving captions describe the images as the first photographs received from the stricken district.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference and excerpt on the 1931 earthquake anniversary
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Neville)
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese observances of the Great Kantō Earthquake anniversary and a new earthquake near Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Memorial services throughout the Tokyo district marked the anniversary of the great earthquake. A strong earthquake on the preceding day reportedly killed twelve people near Tokyo and slightly damaged masonry at the American Embassy.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on evacuation of Japanese residents from Manchuria
subfiles.from: United States Legation, Riga (Robert P. Skinner)
subfiles.about: Directs readers to a despatch concerning Soviet mediation for Japanese civilians detained in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a Riga despatch filed under Manchurian affairs. It notes that General Su agreed to a Soviet request for evacuation of peaceful Japanese residents.

subfiles.title: Despatch on evacuation of Japanese nationals from Manchuria
subfiles.from: Robert P. Skinner, United States Legation, Riga
subfiles.about: Forwards a TASS account of negotiations to evacuate Japanese nationals from Manchuria into Soviet territory.
subfiles.summary: The despatch states that Japan asked Soviet authorities at Manzhouli to secure General Su Bingwen's permission for detained Japanese civilians to leave. It encloses the favorable Chinese reply and notes distribution of copies to Tokyo, Peiping, and Paris.

subfiles.title: TASS account of negotiations with General Su Bingwen
subfiles.from: TASS, as published in Moscow Izvestiya
subfiles.about: Describes Soviet efforts to obtain the release and evacuation of Japanese civilians held by anti-Manchukuo forces.
subfiles.summary: The account says Chinese forces detained Japanese residents after moving against Manchukuo and initially refused evacuation through Manzhouli. Following Soviet intervention, Su Bingwen agreed that women and children could leave first, followed by men who had not participated in military activity or Manchukuo institutions.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet for the 1932 typhoon inquiry
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: Identifies the telegram concerning property damage from a typhoon in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The filing sheet links the calamities file to the Department's telegram requesting information about the storm. It identifies Grew and the November 15 date.

subfiles.title: Instruction requesting a report on typhoon casualties and damage
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Orders the Embassy to report briefly on casualties and damage throughout Japan after the typhoon.
subfiles.summary: The Department asks for a concise national assessment of losses. The message initiated the subsequent exchange about whether official condolences were warranted.

subfiles.title: Internal memorandum on a proposed sympathy instruction
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Seeks a prompt decision on sending a carefully limited expression of sympathy after the typhoon.
subfiles.summary: The writer reports that Castle favored the proposal in principle. The draft intentionally avoided involving the President or Secretary personally, and a decision was requested that evening.

subfiles.title: Preliminary report on the November 1932 typhoon
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Provides initial casualty and damage estimates for the typhoon affecting Tokyo and the Ryukyu Islands.
subfiles.summary: Authorities reported 52 known deaths and 62 missing in the Tokyo region, with further fishing-village losses possible. Grew described property damage in Tokyo as mostly minor and concluded that, although violent, the storm was not a major calamity.

subfiles.title: Letter acknowledging information about Ethiopian relief funds
subfiles.from: John H. Shaw, Ethiopian Consul General, New York
subfiles.to: Paul H. Alling, Department of State
subfiles.about: Thanks Alling for information concerning Shaw's acceptance of donated Ethiopian relief funds.
subfiles.summary: Shaw acknowledges Alling's July 18 letter and expresses appreciation for its guidance. The document is unrelated to the Japanese disaster correspondence and appears to have been misfiled.

subfiles.title: Authorization to convey sympathy after the 1932 typhoon
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Authorizes the Embassy, at its discretion, to express American sympathy for typhoon losses.
subfiles.summary: The proposed message conveyed the American government's sympathy to Japan for loss of life and property. Delivery was left to the Embassy's judgment in light of local circumstances.

subfiles.title: Grew's recommendation against delivering the sympathy message
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Recommends withholding the typhoon condolence message unless later reports reveal much greater losses.
subfiles.summary: Grew argues that similar storms frequently struck Japan and that the recent event did not appear to be a major catastrophe. He feared an official message could be misunderstood and promised to report if it was later delivered.

subfiles.title: Departmental note on final typhoon casualties
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes the final reported typhoon death toll and the absence of notable damage in the Ryukyu Islands.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum cites Tokyo's despatch reporting 273 total deaths. It adds that the Ryukyu Islands apparently suffered no notable damage despite early reports.

subfiles.title: Final report on typhoon damage in Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.about: Presents final casualty and property-loss statistics for the November 14 typhoon and explains why condolences were withheld.
subfiles.summary: Final figures listed 131 known deaths, 142 missing, 376 injured, thousands of damaged or inundated buildings, and 1,406 damaged vessels. Treating the missing as dead gave a toll of 273, principally in Shizuoka, Kanagawa, and Fukushima; Grew concluded that the storm was not exceptional enough to justify delivering the authorized condolence message.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference sheet on the Hakodate fire
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Joseph C. Grew)
subfiles.about: Identifies Grew's telegram reporting the destruction of Hakodate by fire.
subfiles.summary: The sheet characterizes the Hakodate fire as a major catastrophe. It records preliminary reports that the city was completely destroyed and 1,500 people had died.

subfiles.title: Telegram on the destruction of Hakodate
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports American condolences and preliminary information about the catastrophic Hakodate fire.
subfiles.summary: Grew personally conveyed United States government condolences to the Japanese Foreign Minister. Press bulletins reported complete destruction and 1,500 deaths, while the status of American residents remained under investigation because direct communications had failed.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on disaster-stricken emigrants to Brazil
subfiles.from: American Consulate, Kobe (McClintock)
subfiles.about: Refers to a report explaining that emigrants to Brazil came from drought-, fire-, and famine-stricken Japanese districts.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references an emigration report filed elsewhere. It says many settlers bound for Brazil came from areas recently affected by disaster, especially famine-ridden districts of Tōhoku.

subfiles.title: Initial report on the July 1935 Shizuoka earthquake
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports preliminary information on Americans in the Shizuoka earthquake area.
subfiles.summary: The damaged portion of the telegram indicates that Boyce was checking American residents and property. Fifty-four Americans were registered in the area, including thirty-one of Japanese ancestry, and Boyce planned to inspect Shizuoka the next day.

subfiles.title: Follow-up telegram on the Shizuoka earthquake
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports the results of Boyce's visit to Shizuoka after the earthquake.
subfiles.summary: Boyce found no American casualties or damage to American property. Total losses were estimated at ten million yen, with ten deaths.

subfiles.title: Internal note questioning the report's treatment of dual nationality
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Questions the assumption that Japanese-American minors in Shizuoka possessed dual nationality.
subfiles.summary: The writer calls attention to the Shizuoka earthquake report and expresses puzzlement over its reference to dual nationality. The note argues that Americans of Japanese ancestry who had divested themselves of Japanese nationality should be presumed not to retain it.

subfiles.title: Earthquake at Shizuoka and Shimizu
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Provides a fuller account of the July 11 earthquake and efforts to verify the safety of registered Americans.
subfiles.summary: Boyce describes his inspection of Shizuoka and reports no known American deaths or property losses. Registration records listed 54 Americans, including 31 Japanese-American minors whose status required further checking; damage was concentrated in older, poorly built native dwellings, while newer structures survived.

subfiles.title: Enclosure copy of Boyce's July 12 telegram
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reproduces Boyce's preliminary telegram concerning Americans in the Shizuoka earthquake area.
subfiles.summary: The copy reports little or no American property damage and refers to the registered American population. It also records Boyce's intention to visit Shizuoka, with Raymond P. Ludden identified as the encoding vice consul.

subfiles.title: Enclosure copy of Boyce's July 14 telegram
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reproduces the telegram confirming the absence of American casualties or property damage.
subfiles.summary: The message records Boyce's visit to Shizuoka and reports ten deaths and damage estimated at ten million yen. Alvin T. Rowe Jr. encoded and certified the copy.

subfiles.title: List of American residents registered in the Shizuoka area
subfiles.from: American Consulate, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Lists registered Americans and their households or relatives in the Shizuoka consular area.
subfiles.summary: The surviving pages contain names, addresses, ages, and family information for American residents, many of Japanese ancestry. The list states that 54 persons and 35 registrations were recorded for 1933 through 1935, and marks certain residents who were telegraphed for reports on casualties and property damage.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference and extract on the 1935 Taiwan earthquake
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Tokyo (Edwin L. Neville)
subfiles.about: Records press casualty estimates for the July 17 earthquake in Taiwan.
subfiles.summary: The extract states that another earthquake struck Taiwan on July 17. The Japan Times estimated 35 deaths and 131 injuries.

subfiles.title: Telegram on the February 1936 Kansai earthquake
subfiles.from: Krentz, American Consulate, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports a moderate earthquake affecting Kobe, Osaka, and Kyoto.
subfiles.summary: The February 21 shocks caused eight deaths and moderate property damage. No Americans were affected.

subfiles.title: Telegram on American interests in the Osarizawa disaster
subfiles.from: Garrels, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: States that no American lives or property were involved in the Osarizawa disaster.
subfiles.summary: The brief message addresses only American exposure to the disaster. It confirms that neither American persons nor property were affected.

subfiles.title: Grew's telegram on the 1938 Tokyo floods
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains why Grew did not emulate the British Ambassador's official expression of sympathy for Tokyo flood losses.
subfiles.summary: The floods had reportedly killed 134 people, but Grew declined to convey official sympathy because he viewed them as minor compared with Japanese-inflicted civilian suffering in China. He proposed instead to make a quiet personal relief contribution jointly with Mrs. Grew and reported the issue in case it attracted American press attention.

subfiles.title: Departmental approval of Grew's position
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Approves the position taken in Grew's telegram concerning the Tokyo floods.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends a very brief reply stating that it approves. The reference links the approval directly to Grew's July 2 flood telegram.

subfiles.title: First telegram on the catastrophic Kobe flood
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports severe flooding at Kobe, heavy damage, more than 100 deaths, and the apparent safety of Americans.
subfiles.summary: McConaughy initially attributes the disaster to torrential rain and a reported failure of Nunobiki Reservoir. He warns that property damage will be high and promises additional information.

subfiles.title: Correction concerning the Nunobiki Reservoir
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Corrects the initial report that Nunobiki Reservoir had burst.
subfiles.summary: Police denied that the main reservoir failed, suggesting instead that smaller dams and saturated hills released the water. Casualty figures had changed little, and there were still no known American deaths.

subfiles.title: Relayed detailed telegram on the July 5 Kobe flood
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe, via Frank P. Lockhart in Shanghai
subfiles.about: Describes the Kobe flood as a catastrophe and reports casualties, infrastructure failure, and damage to the consulate.
subfiles.summary: Known prefectural casualties totaled 680, including 174 dead, while property losses were already estimated at several million yen. Transport and utilities had collapsed, the consulate basement was inundated, and the worst destruction stretched from Shioya through Kobe, but investigation found no American casualties and little serious American property damage.

subfiles.title: Updated casualty and damage estimate for Kobe
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Updates the official flood death toll, damage estimate, restoration work, and health concerns.
subfiles.summary: The official death toll had reached 900 and the preliminary damage estimate was 100 million yen. Utilities were being restored, but water service remained deficient and officials feared epidemics and additional rain.

subfiles.title: Corrected and duplicate copies of the telegram on flood censorship
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Reports efforts to minimize Kobe flood damage and restrict unauthorized photography.
subfiles.summary: McConaughy says local publicity acknowledged the damage but unauthorized flood photographs were prohibited. He suggests the military may have sought to sustain morale and excuse its limited use of nearby troops, including forces bound for China, in rehabilitation work.

subfiles.title: Departmental paraphrase of McConaughy's flood-censorship telegram
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.about: Paraphrases McConaughy's report about censorship and the military's limited role in Kobe relief.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase states that authorities were attempting to minimize the disaster and forbidding unauthorized photographs. It repeats the suggestion that the policy aimed to bolster morale and justify withholding troops from rehabilitation work.

subfiles.title: Request for a consular contribution to Kobe flood relief
subfiles.from: Gourley, American Consulate, Kobe
subfiles.about: Requests a special allotment of $100 or $150 for donation to Kobe's flood-relief work.
subfiles.summary: The request emphasizes that municipal workers pumped out the consulate basement and cleared deep mud from adjoining streets. Because other foreign consulates had contributed, the sender argues that an American donation would avoid conspicuous nonparticipation and produce a favorable local reaction.

subfiles.title: Authorization of a $150 Kobe relief contribution
subfiles.from: Cordell Hull, Department of State
subfiles.about: Authorizes a $150 allotment for the consulate's contribution to Kobe flood relief.
subfiles.summary: The Department grants the requested $150 and instructs the consul to draw and account for it separately. The authorization number was to be noted on the draft.

subfiles.title: Memorandum supporting use of the Emergency Fund
subfiles.from: Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Recommends approving $150 from the Emergency Fund for Kobe flood relief.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum calls the amount a token but stresses the special municipal help given to the consulate and donations made by other countries' consulates. It notes precedents for such use of the Emergency Fund and reports that Messersmith favored approval.

subfiles.title: Division summary of the Kobe flood report
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes McConaughy's detailed despatch on flood damage in Kobe and Hyōgo Prefecture.
subfiles.summary: The note reports no American deaths and negligible American property losses, while total prefectural damage was estimated at 234.78 million yen. It concludes that Japan would not be appreciably weakened economically or militarily and notes the sparse use of troops in rescue and reconstruction.

subfiles.title: Flood damage in Kobe, Japan, and vicinity
subfiles.from: Walter P. McConaughy, American Consul, Kobe
subfiles.about: Provides a comprehensive confidential analysis of the causes, casualties, losses, health effects, economic consequences, relief measures, and censorship associated with the Kobe flood.
subfiles.summary: McConaughy attributes the disaster to extraordinary rainfall, saturated hills, constrained river channels, urban reclamation, debris blockages, and denuded slopes, while confirming that the American community escaped serious harm. He argues that official casualty figures were deliberately understated, citing secret recovery of bodies from the Hanshin subway and foreign estimates far above the published toll. The report places Hyōgo losses at 234.76 million yen, describes 150,000 homeless people, severe water contamination and dysentery risks, and months of clearance and reconstruction. Although Japan's national military and economic capacity was not seriously weakened, the flood strained labor, capital, factories, public utilities, and local morale; the report also criticizes the limited use of military forces and restrictions on photographs.

subfiles.title: Photographic enclosure captions for Kobe flood damage
subfiles.from: American Consulate, Kobe
subfiles.about: Begins the caption list for photographs documenting flood damage in Kitano-chō, Kobe.
subfiles.summary: The captions identify exposed foundations and ruined houses belonging to or near Walter P. McConaughy, W. Seidel, and Affeld. They also describe views along Kitano-chō and debris piled approximately twenty-five feet high; the enclosure continues beyond this section.
